breadcrumb.name: Amps to Watts Calculator (DC, AC and 3-Phase)

sections.h2: One amp is how many watts?
p: It depends on the voltage. On 230 V mains with a heating load, one amp is 230 W. On a 12 V battery, one amp is just 12 W. For motors and ACs, multiply by the power factor as well, so one amp delivers less real power than the volts suggest.

sections.h2: How many watts can a circuit or breaker handle?
p: Multiply the breaker's amps by the voltage. A 16 A circuit on 230 V carries 3,680 VA, which is 3,680 W of heaters but only 2,944 W of motors and ACs at a power factor of 0.8. The chart below lists the common breaker sizes.

That figure is the ceiling, not a target. A load that runs for hours should stay well under it: the wiring calculators on this site size cables at 1.25 times the running current, and starting surges of motors and compressors come on top.

Choose three-phase and enter the current in one line. The calculator uses the line-to-line voltage (400 V in Pakistan) and the square root of three: 10 A per line at a power factor of 0.8 is 5,543 W. If you know the kW and need the current, the 3 phase amps calculator works the other way.

sections.h2: Watts versus VA: why there are two answers
p: Volts × amps gives volt-amperes (VA), the apparent power the cable and breaker carry. Real watts are VA × power factor, the power that turns into heat, light or motion and that the meter counts. For a heater both are equal; for a motor the watts are lower. UPS and generator ratings in VA or kVA follow the same rule.

faq.a: 230 W on a 230 V supply with a heating load. With a power factor of 0.8 (motors, mixed loads) it is less, and on a 12 V battery one amp is only 12 W.
2,300 W at 230 V with a power factor of one, or 2.3 kW.

faq.q: How many watts is 16 A at 230 V?
faq.a: 3,680 W for heating loads and 2,944 W at a power factor of 0.8. A 16 A socket circuit can carry one large heater or AC, but not several at once.

faq.q: How many watts can a 15 amp circuit handle?
faq.a: At 120 V the ceiling is 1,800 W for heating loads. Loads that run for hours should stay well below it, and motors and ACs need room for their starting surge.

faq.q: What is the amps to watts formula?
faq.a: Watts = volts × amps for DC; watts = volts × amps × power factor for single-phase AC; watts = √3 × line-to-line volts × amps × power factor for three-phase.

faq.q: How do I convert amps to watts on three-phase?
faq.a: Multiply √3 × line-to-line volts × the current in one line × power factor. 10 A per line at 400 V and a power factor of 0.8 is 5,543 W.

faq.q: How many watts is 20 amps at 12 V DC?
faq.a: 240 W. On DC the watts are simply volts × amps, with no power factor.

key_facts: Watts = amps × volts × power factor. 16 A at 230 V and a power factor of 0.8 is 2,944 W, out of 3,680 VA of apparent power.
One amp on a 230 V supply carries 230 W of heating load; on a 12 V battery one amp carries only 12 W.
A 15 A circuit at 120 V (common in the US) carries at most 1,800 W of heating load before the breaker's rating is reached.
On three-phase, 10 A per line at 400 V and a power factor of 0.8 is 5,543 W, because three lines share the load.
mistakes: Multiplying amps by volts for a motor or AC and calling it watts. That is VA; the real watts are lower by the power factor (about 0.8).
Loading a circuit right up to the watts in the chart. Those are ceilings; a heater or AC running for hours should leave a margin, and motors surge above their running current at start-up.
Using 230 V with the three-phase formula. Three-phase uses the line-to-line voltage (400 V) and the square root of three, with the current of one line.
Copying a US chart for a 230 V supply. The same amps carry about twice the watts at 230 V as at 120 V, so always use the voltage of your own supply.

how.tpl: {{out.k|4}} × {{in.amps}} A × {{out.volts}} V × {{out.pf|2}} power factor = {{out.watts|int}} W ({{out.kw|2}} kW). The first factor is one for DC and single-phase and √3 for three-phase, where the volts are line-to-line and the amps are per line. Without the power factor the result is {{out.va|int}} VA, the apparent power the wires carry. On DC the power factor is one.
how.text: 1 × 16 A × 230 V × 0.8 power factor = 2,944 W (2.94 kW). The first factor is one for DC and single-phase and √3 for three-phase, where the volts are line-to-line and the amps are per line. Without the power factor the result is 3,680 VA, the apparent power the wires carry. On DC the power factor is one.

examples.title: 1 amp at 230 V: how many watts?
examples.text: 1 A × 230 V × 1 = 230 W for a heating load. With a power factor below one, the same amp carries fewer real watts.

examples.title: 10 amps to watts at 230 V
examples.text: 10 A × 230 V × 1 = 2,300 W (2.3 kW). That is roughly one large room heater or a kettle and an iron together.

examples.title: How many watts can a 15 A circuit at 120 V handle?
examples.text: 15 A × 120 V × 1 = 1,800 W at most for heating loads. Long-running loads should stay well below this so the cable and breaker do not run at their limit.

examples.title: 20 amps from a 12 V battery
examples.text: 20 A × 12 V = 240 W. DC has no power factor, so the watts are simply volts times amps.

examples.title: 10 amps per line on three-phase 400 V
examples.text: √3 × 400 V × 10 A × 0.8 = 5,543 W (5.54 kW). The apparent power is 6,928 VA.

content.answer: 16 amps on a 230 V single-phase supply is 2,944 watts at a power factor of 0.8, and 3,680 W for a heater with a power factor of one. Watts = amps × volts × power factor; DC uses a power factor of one, and three-phase multiplies by the square root of three.

formula.text: DC: P = V × I;  single-phase AC: P = V × I × PF;  three-phase AC: P = √3 × V × I × PF
lines: P = real power in watts (W); kW = W ÷ 1,000
I = current in amps (A), per line for three-phase
V = voltage: battery voltage for DC, phase-to-neutral for single-phase, line-to-line for three-phase
PF = power factor between 0 and 1; V × I without PF is the apparent power in VA

content.safety: The watts a breaker allows are a ceiling for the circuit, not permission to add loads. Before putting a heater, AC or motor on an existing circuit, check the cable size with the wire size calculator and have a licensed electrician confirm the circuit.
